However, a storm surge in this region is unlikely to reach 15.48 feet above MLLW which would be necessary to flood the site. Hurricane Helene in 2024 created a record storm surge reported to be 7.2 feet above MLLW in nearby East Bay. That broke the previous record of 4.56 feet set the previous year by Hurricane Idalia, a Category 4 hurricane off Tampa’s coast. The site is still approximately 8 feet higher than this record storm surge event. Hurricane-strength winds are also a risk throughout this region of the United States. Ensuring that all equipment and materials are suitable for saltwater environments to the extent practical will also be part of future detailed design phases. 3.3 PROXIMITY TO EXISTING CO SOURCES & DESTINATIONS 2 There are numerous types of CO emission sources in the West Central region of Florida, all of which could 2 be served by the T-RICH hub. This section summarizes those source types in order of decreasing priority for this project. We have identified electricity generating power plants as the highest priority, due to them having the greatest point source quantities of emissions compared to all other emitter types. Power plants in the region tend to have annual CO emissions greater than 500,000 tons, and even up to 4.2 million 2 tons, compared to other industrial types of emitters whose annual CO emissions generally tend to remain 2 under 125,000 tons. Therefore, it would likely be the most cost-effective option, and the greatest positive benefit to the environment and human health, to install carbon capture systems at power plants and transport that CO to T-RICH. At the other end of the spectrum, a small but increasingly important emitting 2 category are marine cargo vessels that capture CO from their exhaust gas and store it onboard until they 2 reach port. Once they reach a port, they will need a facility like T-RICH to discharge it to. The International Maritime Organization has issued regulations for shipping companies to reduce their vessels’ carbon emissions. Onboard carbon capture systems are being developed and tested to meet these emission regulations. In the future, as more ships install these onboard systems, the demand for port terminals like T-RICH to offload the captured gas has the potential to become a significant terminal activity. Such vessels are expected to transfer less than 1,000 tons of CO per ship visit.
